question: What are the most common reasons prospects hesitate to buy?
correct_reason: Five of the six required themes are supported and none is contradicted. The licensing and usage model theme is the only one missing.

verdicts.reason: Says budget and price are a common hesitation, citing annual cost and approval thresholds, but names none of the specific companies' price gaps.
Covers the internal-build and existing-tool alternatives: expanding the Workato contract, Zapier plus process discipline, and building internally.
Names integration effort as a recurring blocker but omits SAP, Dynamics and iManage.
Says security and legal requirements are gates, citing the BAA and UK residency confirmation.
Only briefly mentions seat minimums; it does not cover occasional-approver seats, usage overages or subflow billing.
Quotes 'Maintenance and observability are the real costs' and says the operational burden may outweigh the value.

answer.summary: The most common hesitations are security/legal gating, pricing or budget, and the fear that the work is better built or handled internally. Across the calls, prospects also repeatedly hesitate over AI features, integration/maintenance complexity, and whether the product is simply not worth replacing an existing process or tool. These are prospect-side concerns, not OrbitFlow claims, and several calls frame them as hard gates rather than soft objections.

[08:09] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's closer to how we'd think about it. I'd be nervous if the proposal was migrate everything.

[09:16] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yeah, go.
[09:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's exactly the right level to test at, and it's the bit I'd want you to push on. Workflows are event-driven but each run holds state. [09:40] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can the queue be owned by a team? Not a named person. People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.
[...]
[13:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run. [13:23] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'd want that in the evaluation. A demo with clean data proves nothing to me.
[13:30] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Agreed. Give us dirty data.
[13:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): On integrations — you'd said Salesforce is mandatory, Slack and Snowflake matter for phase one, Gainsight would be useful but isn't essential. Which one's the deal-breaker?
[13:48] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The system of record. If that connector's unreliable, none of the rest matters. After that it's the collaboration and data systems, because that's where context goes missing.
[14:02] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): For your stack it's a mix of native connectors and API-based options. What I'd want to do in a pilot is validate each required operation rather than just point at a logo on our integrations page.
[14:17] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Good.
[14:19] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): One thing I noted from your pre-call form — you've got roughly a hundred and forty customer-facing users but you'd only expect twenty-five to actually build or administer workflows?
[...]
[18:36] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Can we get metrics out into our own monitoring? I don't want operationally critical automation only visible inside a vendor console.
[18:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise. Several customers forward failures into their incident tooling. Happy to show actual payloads in a technical session.
[...]
[20:05] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's fine. Baseline is SOC 2 Type II. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Audit logs cover administrative and workflow events. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU residency available on Enterprise if you ever need it.

question: What concerns did customers raise about pricing?
correct_reason: The answer covers the seat-cost concern, usage unpredictability, professional-services transparency and, loosely, the high price. It misses the internal sign-off thresholds and Fable Media's request for 10 users or monthly billing.

verdicts.reason: The answer says one customer found the headline price higher than they expected, and another compared it with a much cheaper existing tool. It does not name the Growth plan, the 1,800 figure, or any of the companies' expected amounts, so this support is loose.
The answer never mentions internal sign-off or approval thresholds.

The answer states the occasional-approver seat concern and cites CALL-001, 002, 004, 008 and 009. These appear to be Acme, BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Harbor Legal and Inkwell, although the answer gives call IDs rather than company names.
The answer covers unpredictable usage bills and mentions the second-year invoice, citing CALL-005 (Ember). It does not mention Juniper or Lumen.
The answer does not mention Fable Media wanting 10 users or monthly billing.
The answer cites the CALL-004 request for transparency on professional services and premium connectors.

Power Automate is described as the bundled tool from a Microsoft deal, with BrightPath named explicitly. The other calls are not clearly tied to company names.
MuleSoft is described as the integration backbone they already own, with the cheaper alternative being MuleSoft plus custom integration services.
Make (tested for branching), Retool Workflows and Step Functions are mentioned. Gainsight is mentioned, but not as an expansion option.

[01:29] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The short version is we've got too much operational work living between systems. And I want to be clear up front, we're not looking for another dashboard. We've got dashboards. We need something that actually moves work along and makes it visible who owns what.
[...]
[01:51] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Sure. Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success. All of that is managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders. So renewal risks and implementation blockers get noticed late. Not never — late.
[...]
[08:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay, so let me try one. If we picked a single workflow for phase one — opportunity closes in Salesforce, create the onboarding plan, assign tasks based on product mix, notify the right Slack channel, escalate stalled milestones up to CS leadership. Is that the right shape?
[...]
[09:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's exactly the right level to test at, and it's the bit I'd want you to push on. Workflows are event-driven but each run holds state. So you can branch on data, pause for approvals, retry external actions, set timeout rules, and push an exception into a queue rather than just failing quietly.
[...]
[11:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right. So left-hand side is triggers and actions, middle is the flow, right-hand panel is the config for whatever step you've selected. A workflow can start from a SaaS event, a schedule, a webhook, a database query, or another workflow.
[...]
[15:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You'd mentioned AI in your notes. I'll be brief on it because I don't think it's the centre of gravity here. We treat it as optional steps inside a workflow rather than making the whole product autonomous. Classification, summarisation, extracting fields from text, drafting something for a human to approve.
[...]
[15:43] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Rules for anything already structured and safety-critical. Model where the input is genuinely unstructured or the task is semantic. Summarising a long ticket thread, fine. Deciding whether to issue a refund above a threshold — that should stay deterministic and permissioned.
[...]
[17:19] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): For anything customer-facing or exec-facing I'd want a link back to the underlying records. People need to be able to challenge the output.
[...]
[17:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Let me show you run history, actually, because it's related. [pause] So — filter by workflow, status, time, or a business field. Open a run, you get every step, inputs, outputs, timing, retries, any human approval.
[...]
[27:38] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Approval forms can collect structured inputs and those values feed subsequent steps. For heavily customised forms some customers use their own front end and call us through the API.

[06:21] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): The process people describe and the process people run are not always the same thing.

[09:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's exactly the right level to test at, and it's the bit I'd want you to push on. Workflows are event-driven but each run holds state. [09:53] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And the run history persists, so an admin can see the inputs, which steps ran, where it stopped.

[10:12] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): There's a second use case I'd flag, not for phase one — identifying renewal risk by combining CRM fields, support activity and product usage signals out of Snowflake. [10:31] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It doesn't. Different shape of workflow — that's more scheduled and query-driven than event-driven — but same platform.

[11:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right. So left-hand side is triggers and actions, middle is the flow, right-hand panel is the config for whatever step you've selected. A workflow can start from a SaaS event, a schedule, a webhook, a database query, or another workflow.

[12:12] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah, that's fair criticism and I'm not going to pretend. Simple mapping and branching is visual. Transformations use expressions. [15:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You'd mentioned AI in your notes. I'll be brief on it because I don't think it's the centre of gravity here. [15:43] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Rules for anything already structured and safety-critical. Model where the input is genuinely unstructured or the task is semantic. [17:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Let me show you run history, actually, because it's related. [pause] So — filter by workflow, status, time, or a business field. Open a run, you get every step, inputs, outputs, timing, retries, any human approval.

[19:04] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Version history — if someone changes a condition on a Friday afternoon and it breaks, can we see exactly what changed?

[19:40] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): It is, relatively. We need the usual vendor review, SSO, audit logs. We don't have a special data-residency requirement for this project.
[...]
[23:18] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true. [24:47] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): With naming conventions. And change control on the important ones. And a rule that somebody other than the creator can understand each production flow.

[27:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Can a human modify data before approving? Sometimes approval isn't just yes or no.
[27:38] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Approval forms can collect structured inputs and those values feed subsequent steps. For heavily customised forms some customers use their own front end and call us through the API.
[27:52] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Last one. Can we trigger a workflow manually for a one-off exception?
[27:58] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes, permissions allowing. It's useful during migration and for exception recovery.

answer.summary: Taking Acme Corp to mean Acme Logistics, the call says their current workflow is fragmented across systems, spreadsheets, Slack reminders, and ad hoc automations, with gaps between automated steps and late visibility into risks and blockers. They also said the process people describe is not always the process they run: onboarding is standardized on paper, but EMEA and North America actually use different milestone definitions. The main pain is not that everything is manual, but that coordination, ownership, change control, and exception handling are inconsistent.

answer.summary: Across these two churn calls, customers left mainly because the product did not fit the way they were actually operating: Verity Payments found it needed an engineering-style owner and custom support, while Oakhill Property found the product was more expensive than the value of the workflows it was using. In both cases, the original sales story depended on a future that did not materialize — more internal capacity at Verity, and more workflows/process improvement at Oakhill. Timing also mattered: both customers had already moved on or were evaluating alternatives by the time OrbitFlow tried to help.

The renewal calls are much more explicit about seat counts, run tiers, term length, and support issues; the new-business calls are more about problem fit and what evidence is needed next.

=== CALL-003 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-003
DATE: 2026-06-11
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Cedar & Finch
INDUSTRY: E-commerce
COMPANY SIZE: 180 employees
STAGE: Discovery / demo
DURATION: 17 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Sophie Reed, Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch
- Marcus Lee, Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch
TRANSCRIPT
[00:25] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): We've done three of these in a fortnight. I can recite our own pain points. Can we just see it and I'll interrupt when something matters?
[...]
[01:20] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've pre-built something that I think is roughly your world. High-value order comes in, there's a fulfilment exception on it, we open a ticket, we ping a channel, we update a tracker.
[...]
[02:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Good. So — this branch here. If the required fields aren't populated it doesn't just carry on, it drops into an exception queue.
[02:17] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Owned by who?
[...]
[02:37] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Tell him the number.
[02:39] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Right, so. We've got more than sixty Zapier automations. Six-zero. And several of them are owned by people who don't work here any more.
[02:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How do you find out when one breaks?
[02:53] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): When a customer complains.
[02:56] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] Right.
[02:59] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): That's not a joke, that's genuinely the detection mechanism.
[03:04] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): It's the honest answer.
[03:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's a very common answer. It's just usually not said out loud in the first ten minutes.
[03:14] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Well, we're not going to fix it by pretending.
[03:18] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No. Okay, so let me show you the bit that speaks to that. [pause] This is run history. Filter by workflow, status, time. Open any run and you see every step, the inputs, the outputs, timings, retries.
[03:36] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Can I set an alert on a failure rate rather than an individual failure? Because sixty automations, if I get an email per failure I'll just filter them into a folder and never look at it.
[03:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes — you can alert when error rates cross a threshold. And that's the right instinct, everyone who alerts per-failure ends up ignoring all of them.
[04:01] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Learned that one the hard way.
[04:05] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Can I correct something Sophie said in the email, actually?
[04:09] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Go on.
[04:11] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): I think I may have overstated the Zendesk angle earlier. Support feels like the loudest problem because failures surface there — that's where the customer shouts. But honestly, probably only about a quarter of the automations actually touch Zendesk.
[...]
[04:37] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Shopify mostly. Klaviyo. Some Airtable stuff.
[04:42] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Let me give you the full list. Shopify, Zendesk, Klaviyo, Slack, Airtable, and Zapier holding it all together with string.
[...]
[04:58] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Shopify. A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
[...]
[05:53] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): We need a standard DPA. SSO would be nice rather than mandatory — we're a hundred and eighty people, I'm not going to pretend we've got a zero-trust programme. And because we sell into the UK and EU I want to understand where customer data actually gets processed.
[06:14] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That last one I can answer partly. EU data residency is available on Enterprise. On Growth, I'd need to confirm the default processing region for you in writing rather than guess.
[...]
[07:30] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Ours? About two hundred and something. But that's not the comparison and you know it, because the two hundred doesn't include the four hours a week you spend chasing broken ones.
[...]
[08:01] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): I genuinely don't know. Nobody's ever asked me to count it.
[...]
[09:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Version history and change metadata on every workflow. So you can see what changed and when. And you'd typically define who can publish to production versus who can build in a dev workspace.
[...]
[10:05] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): We do, but I'd underplay it for you. It's optional steps inside a workflow — classification, summarisation, extracting fields out of text, drafting something a human then approves. It's not an autonomous agent thing.
[...]
[10:42] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a reasonable fit — summarise the week's tickets by theme, with links back to the underlying tickets so someone can check it.
[10:52] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): With links. Because I don't trust a summary I can't verify.
[...]
[12:47] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Honestly? Zapier and Make. I like Zapier for the simple stuff, it does what it says. And I've tested Make for the more complicated branching, which it handles better than I expected.
[...]
[16:32] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Actually, yeah, one. If we did buy this, do we have to migrate all sixty at once?

[00:43] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Error rate's sitting at one point four percent, which is down from four point one when you started. Most of that improvement came in April.

[01:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I know, but it counts.

[01:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Yes. Median time from exception raised to first action is now forty minutes. It was — Devan, what was it before?
[01:20] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Between two and six hours, depending on who was on.
[01:24] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Six hours was optimistic.
[01:27] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): [laughs] Six hours was the number we admitted to.
[01:31] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): That's the one that's changed how the depots work. Genuinely. I had a depot manager tell me in July that he'd stopped keeping his own spreadsheet, and that's — you don't get that often.
[01:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's the metric I'd actually put in front of your board, for what it's worth. Not the run counts.
[01:54] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): I already have.
[01:57] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Good. Now the less pleasant part of the numbers.
[02:02] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Overages.
[02:03] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Overages. You've exceeded your contracted run volume in four of the last six months. June was twenty-two percent over.
[02:13] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): We knew. We've been watching it.
[02:16] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Were we charged for those?

[02:39] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): I knew about March. I didn't know about May.
[02:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): May was a judgement call. I'd rather tell you now than have it look like a discovery in the renewal.
[02:51] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Appreciated. But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
[02:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The run tier is wrong, yes. Which is most of what I want to talk about.

[04:10] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Fine.

[07:31] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): [pause] Yes. Let's do that.
[07:35] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Would that be a lot of runs?

[18:15] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): From me — the retry configuration session with Devan, the subprocessor list for Priyanka, a short note on what the supplier onboarding instrumentation phase would look like, and the named SAP escalation contact.

=== CALL-012 (call kind: renewal)
CALL ID: CALL-012

TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Morning Graham, morning Nadia. Thanks for making the time — I know this one's been rescheduled twice.

[00:46] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then tell me. Start wherever you want.
[00:50] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): The honest answer is that I inherited this. Ravi bought it, Ravi implemented it, Ravi left in February, and I picked it up in March with about forty minutes of handover.
[01:05] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Forty minutes.
[01:07] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Forty minutes and a Confluence page that was last edited in November.
[01:13] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): The Confluence page is quite good, in fairness.

[...]

=== CALL-002 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-002
DATE: 2026-06-05
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: BrightPath Health
INDUSTRY: Digital health
COMPANY SIZE: 1,100 employees
STAGE: Technical discovery
DURATION: 34 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Priya Shah, Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health
- Elliot Greene, Security Architect, BrightPath Health
TRANSCRIPT
[06:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What else can we send? SOC 2 report, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation — is that the pack?
[06:42] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Add pen test summary. And yes. And we'll send you our questionnaire, which is long, and I apologise in advance.
[06:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): They're all long. We'll complete it.
[06:58] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): One more. Who at your end can see our run data?
[07:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Role-based access, workspace separation, and secrets are never displayed in run logs. Internally, support access is controlled and logged. If you need field-level masking for specific payloads, that's a design conversation rather than a checkbox.
[07:24] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): We will need that conversation. We have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without seeing the record contents.
[07:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah, that's a very common pattern in your sector. It's designable, I just don't want to say "yes, masking, done" when the real answer is "yes, with design".
[07:48] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Understood. Right, that's most of my list. I've got twenty-five minutes before I have to go. Priya, do you want to do current state so I can hear it?
[08:00] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Yes, let's.
[08:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please. What's actually broken today?
[08:08] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Two things, and they're linked. First, business teams request automations from a small systems group — my group — and there's a growing backlog. Second, compliance review slows down any workflow that touches patient-adjacent data, which is most of them.
[08:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How long's the backlog?
[08:32] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Currently? [pause] I'd say eleven weeks for anything non-trivial. It was six in January.
[08:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So it's getting worse.
[08:44] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): It's getting worse. And what happens when the backlog gets long is people route around us. Someone builds something in Power Automate, it works, they leave, and then it's nobody's.
[08:59] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Which is my problem, eventually.
[09:03] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Which becomes Elliot's problem, eventually, yes.
[09:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is it that the steps are manual, or —
[09:11] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): No, that's the thing. It's not that every step is manual, we have automation in places. The problem is the gaps between the automated pieces. Something fires, then there's a four-day hole where a human is supposed to notice, and sometimes they don't.
[09:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you have telemetry on that or is it anecdotal?
[09:36] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Mix. Outcome metrics exist. Operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same failure happened fifteen times last month.
[...]
[10:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It is. Okay, let me play the stack back. HubSpot, Microsoft Teams, Azure, Databricks, Jira Service Management.
[11:05] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's it. Plus a lot of SharePoint that nobody admits to.
[11:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is the system of record for the process?
[11:15] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Depends on the object. Customer and commercial data has a clear home. Tasks and tickets have a different home. And then a very large amount of actual context lives in chat, which — that's precisely why a workflow layer is interesting to us.
[11:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And you've got Power Automate today.
[11:40] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): We do. It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
[11:48] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So what's the problem with it?
[11:51] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Complex flows are difficult to monitor. And ownership becomes unclear when the creator changes role, which happens constantly. So I want to be clear — I'm not sitting here saying we have no automation. The question is whether a different layer gives us better maintainability and operational control.
[12:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the right question, and we won't try to replace everything. Plenty of customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep integration and use us for business-owned workflows — the ones with human decisions, exceptions, cross-functional handoffs.
[...]
[18:22] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Yes.
[18:24] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): So — triggers and actions on the left, the flow in the middle, config for the selected step on the right. A workflow can start from a SaaS event, a schedule, a webhook, a database query, or another workflow.
[18:41] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll start this one from a record-change event, validate a few required fields, enrich from a second system, then branch. And the thing I want to emphasise, particularly for you given the backlog problem — we push people hard towards small reusable components. If your systems group builds ten good subflows, account lookup, approval, notification, incident creation, then the marginal cost of the eleventh business request drops a lot.
[19:14] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's — okay, that's actually the interesting bit for me. That's the backlog answer, potentially.
[19:23] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It's the one that compounds, yes.
[19:27] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): How technical is it really? Because every vendor says no-code until you hit the one thing the connector doesn't do.
[19:37] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Fair, and I won't pretend. Mapping and branching are visual. Transformations use expressions. On Enterprise you can package reusable JavaScript steps. There's a generic REST action and webhooks. We don't claim every workflow is no-code. The goal is that the workflow stays understandable even when an engineer supplied one custom component.
[...]
[24:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's completely logical and I'm not going to push. What I'd ask is that when we do get to it, you let me build the model around your actual user population rather than a headline number.
[24:53] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): What counts as a user? Because we'd have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or get a notification.
[25:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Builders and full workspace users are the licensed ones. Approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently depending on package. I'm deliberately not quoting you a figure today because without the user model any figure I give is misleading.
[25:23] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Please make that explicit in the proposal when it comes. I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
[25:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It'll be itemised. Assumed builders, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, one-time services separately.
[25:46] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Thank you.
[25:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How would you make the ROI case internally? Headcount, cycle time, errors, engineering maintenance?
[25:58] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Not headcount. I wouldn't sell it that way and it also isn't true. The stronger case is consistency and speed. We've got expensive people doing coordination work because the systems don't carry enough process context. And there's the backlog cost, which is harder to quantify but it's real — eleven weeks of waiting has a number attached to it somewhere.
[26:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For a pilot we can baseline one or two things before automating. Elapsed time, manual touches, exception rate, or systems-group hours spent on requests.
[26:40] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): The last one. That's the one my director cares about.
[26:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then that's the baseline.
[26:48] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I'd also measure adoption. A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation. That's literally what happened with our last internal tool.
[27:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Who owns this day to day if it goes ahead?
[27:07] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I'm the sponsor — business systems. Security can veto, as you've seen. Privacy counsel reviews the DPA and the BAA. Procurement handles final terms.
[27:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Four gates.
[27:24] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Four gates. Welcome to healthcare.
[27:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And operationally?
[...]
[30:20] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Good.
[30:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Concrete next steps then. We send the security pack — SOC 2, subprocessors, DPA, architecture diagram, retention docs, pen test summary. Separately, and this is the one that matters, a written position on the BAA within a week. You send us the representative workflow and some sample data, ideally messy. And we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria.
[30:53] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): And a session on the permission model for Elliot.
[30:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And a session on the permission model for Elliot. Jon, can you own that?
[31:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah. I'd want an hour and I'd want Elliot to bring his worst-case scenario rather than me showing him a clean one.
[31:14] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): He will have one ready. He always has one ready.
[31:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me summarise. You don't need automation for its own sake. The opportunity is a systems group that builds components rather than fulfilling tickets, and a small number of cross-system processes that are observable and less dependent on individuals. The blocker is regulatory, not technical, and until it's answered nothing else moves.
[31:47] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's an accurate summary.
[31:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): One more thing — can you write down the assumptions we made today? Some of what you told me was approximate and I don't want it hardening into a requirement by accident.
[32:04] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): You want me to do that?
[32:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No, sorry — I'll do that. I'll send a recap with open questions separated from confirmed requirements.
[32:16] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Ah. Yes. That would be useful, actually, because half of what I said about the backlog was from memory.
[32:25] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then it goes in the open questions column.
[32:29] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Great. Thanks both. And apologies again for the alarm.
[32:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Genuinely the least disruptive thing that's happened to me this week.
[32:41] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): [laughs] Bye.
[32:44] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Priya.

- Hannah Cole, Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Morning Noah, morning Hannah. Nina's joining in a couple of minutes, she's coming off another call.
[00:07] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): No problem. Shall I set the frame?
[00:11] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[00:13] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): So you should know we're running this as a bake-off. You and Tray.io. We've had a Tray proof of concept running for about six weeks. This isn't a discovery call for us, we know what we want. This is us testing whether you can do it.

[00:39] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Connector breadth is genuinely good. No complaints there.
[00:44] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The engineers hate debugging it.
[00:47] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Hannah's being blunt but she's not wrong. Large visual workflows are hard for our people to reason about. When something goes wrong at step forty of a sixty-step flow, the debugging experience is — it's not good.
[01:04] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a fair criticism of the category, honestly, not just of them. Big visual workflows are hard to debug everywhere. [...]
[01:30] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The other thing you should know is who has to be convinced. I'm the executive sponsor and I'm broadly positive. [03:39] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then my honest answer is: it depends entirely on how you use it, and you have full control over whether you use it at all. [04:07] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Can I have a workspace where they're disabled and another where they aren't?

[...]
[05:39] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then the design principle is that the AI output is a leaf node, not an intermediate value. It gets rendered to a person, it doesn't feed the next branch.

[06:01] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. I'm not going to tell you there's a switch labelled "AI outputs cannot feed decisions", because there isn't.

[06:49] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Retention configurable within supported ranges. [07:17] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The last one — contractual or marketing?
[07:21] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It needs to be contractual for you to rely on it, and I'd expect legal to insist.
[07:28] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): They will.
[07:30] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): On exportable audit history — define exportable. Because I've had vendors mean "you can download a CSV from a UI" and that is not exportable.
[07:43] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [laughs] API and webhook based, so programmatic. Several customers forward failures and audit events into their own tooling continuously rather than pulling reports. That's the pattern I'd recommend for you.
[07:59] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Into our SIEM.
[08:01] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Into your SIEM, yes.
[08:04] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Then that's satisfactory, subject to seeing the actual payload schema.
[08:10] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll send the schema.
[08:13] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Good. That's my two gates addressed at the level a call can address them.
[08:20] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Then let's do the use case, because I want Nina to see how ugly it is.
[08:26] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.

[08:46] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And the problem is auditability.
[08:49] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The problem is auditability and the problem is that four engineers hold the whole thing in their heads. If two of them left in the same quarter we'd be in genuine difficulty.
[09:03] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Three of them are on the same team.
[09:06] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Three of them are on the same team, yes, which is worse.
[09:11] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Do you have telemetry on how often exceptions occur and how long they take?
[09:17] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Partially. We have outcome metrics. Operational telemetry is weak — we can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why, or which dependency failed, or whether the same pattern happened fifteen times last month.
[...]
[10:15] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Okay. So let me play back the phase-one candidate as I understood it. Detect failed or delayed partner onboarding events. Enrich them from Salesforce and Snowflake. Open a Jira incident. And maintain a complete audit trail of approvals and remediation steps.
[...]
[12:24] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Then design standards matter as much as the platform.
[...]
[13:13] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's write it into the criteria.
[13:17] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Let me show the composition point since it came up at the start. [13:41] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Can I unit test a subflow?

[14:19] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It's the debugging loop and it's error handling. Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.

[15:07] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): That's the answer I'd give.
[15:10] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then we agree on the problem, which is a start.

[15:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go.

[15:51] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Not currently.

context.text:
=== CALL-009 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-009
DATE: 2026-08-04
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Inkwell Learning
INDUSTRY: Education technology
COMPANY SIZE: 520 employees
STAGE: Solution evaluation
DURATION: 31 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Olivia Grant, SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning
- Darren Wu, Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Hi Olivia, hi Darren. Olivia, I know you've got a hard stop at half past so I'll keep us moving.
[00:08] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Thank you. I do, unfortunately.
[00:11] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I can stay on after if it's useful.
[00:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That'd be helpful, actually. Where I'd like to start is the use case, because we've had two rounds of email on it and I want to make sure we're solving the same problem.
[00:26] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Yes. So — support volume spikes around school-term launches. Enormously. And the problem isn't the volume itself, we can staff for volume. The problem is that we struggle to distinguish isolated tickets from account-level implementation risk until the escalation reaches an executive.
[00:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So by the time you know, it's already senior.
[00:53] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): By the time I know, a school district's chief of staff has emailed our CEO. That's the current detection mechanism and it is not a good one.
[01:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How often?
[01:07] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Four or five times a term. Which sounds small until you remember each one is a renewal at risk.
[01:16] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Can I complicate this before we go further?
[01:20] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Go ahead, he's going to anyway.
[01:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] I am. So — the proposal, as I understand it, is to combine Zendesk ticket patterns, Salesforce account status, and Snowflake product usage to flag accounts needing proactive intervention, and create structured follow-up tasks.
[01:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's how I've written it down, yes.
[01:44] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Right. And my concern is not whether that's technically possible. It obviously is. My concern is data quality. If Salesforce fields are stale, an elegant workflow will still make bad decisions. Beautifully, consistently, at scale.
[02:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a fair challenge and I'd rather have it now.
[02:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): There's a specific version of it, actually, and I want to challenge something Olivia said in the last session.
[02:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Here we go.
[02:18] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Olivia talks about account-health scores as though they're reliable. Leadership uses them, they're on the QBR deck, they're in the board pack. But fewer than half our CSMs update the underlying fields consistently. So I would not treat those scores as ground truth, and if we build a workflow that keys off them we've automated a guess.
[02:44] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's — I don't entirely disagree.
[02:49] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): You've disagreed before.
[02:52] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I've disagreed with the framing. I think the scores are directionally useful and you think they're noise.
[03:00] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I think they're noise with a trend in them, which is not the same as useful.
[03:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask a question that might be helpful here?
[03:11] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Please.
[03:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Of the three data sources — Zendesk tickets, Salesforce status, Snowflake usage — which one do you both actually trust?
[03:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [immediately] Snowflake.
[03:25] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [crosstalk] Snowflake, yes.
[03:27] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because it's machine-generated. Nobody has to remember to update it.
[03:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Zendesk?
[03:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Reasonably good. Ticket volume and category are reliable. The sentiment tagging is not, because it's manual.
[03:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Salesforce.
[03:47] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Salesforce is reliable for the commercial facts — contract dates, ARR, owner. It is unreliable for anything a human has to remember to type.
[04:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's actually a very clean answer and I think it's the design.
[04:06] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Say more.
[04:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Weight the signals by how they're produced. Machine-generated usage data and structured ticket data carry the flag. Human-maintained fields are context you show to the person, not inputs the logic depends on.
[04:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's — yes. That's the right architecture.
[...]
[05:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You absolutely don't, and you should do it before you buy anything from us.
[...]
[05:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren, could you do that?
[05:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I could do that in a day. Maybe two.
[05:39] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Then why haven't we?
[05:41] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because nobody's asked me to, and because I've been arguing about the health scores instead.
[05:48] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] Fair.
[05:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd suggest making it the first thing, honestly. It's the cheapest way to find out whether this project should exist.
[05:59] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I'm slightly surprised you're saying that.
[06:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): If it turns out the signal isn't there, you'd discover it in month three of a pilot and I'd have burned your goodwill and my quarter. I'd rather know in week one.
[06:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Alright. Darren, do it.
[06:19] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I'll do it.
[06:21] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what you'd look for? Because the answer isn't binary.
[06:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Meaning?
[06:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Meaning it's rarely "the signal was there" or "it wasn't." It's usually "it was there for six of the twelve, and for four of those it was there so early it'd have been indistinguishable from noise."
[06:43] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's a good point. So I'd want the lead time as well as the presence.
[06:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And the false positive rate. How many accounts looked the same and turned out fine.
[06:57] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Yes. That's the harder half.
[...]
[07:04] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because to measure false positives I need to know which accounts were fine, and "fine" isn't recorded anywhere. Absence of escalation isn't the same as fine.
[...]
[09:35] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Go on.
[09:37] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Sharing. [pause] So this is a workflow that's roughly the pattern we're describing. It's scheduled rather than event-driven — it runs daily, queries the warehouse, joins against the CRM, and evaluates a set of conditions.
[09:56] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Where does the query live?
[10:00] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): In the workflow, in this case. But you can also point at a view you own in Snowflake, which for you is probably better.
[10:10] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Much better. I don't want business logic living in two places.
[10:16] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then the pattern is: you own the definition of "at risk" as a view in Snowflake, we consume it and act on it. The intelligence is yours, the orchestration is ours.
[10:30] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's the first time a vendor has said that to me.
[10:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It's the only version that survives contact with a BI team.
[10:40] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It really is.
[10:43] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): What does "act on it" mean concretely?
[10:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): In this flow — create a structured follow-up task with the account, the signal that triggered it, and links back to the underlying tickets and usage. Assign it to the account's CSM, or to a queue if the owner field is stale. Escalate if nothing happens in N days.
[11:09] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): The escalation. That's the bit I want.
[11:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And it's the bit that's usually missing. An alert with no escalation path is a notification, and notifications get ignored.
[11:23] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): They do. I've got a Slack channel full of them.
[11:28] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's my channel and I take that personally.
[11:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] It's not personal, it's just full.
[11:36] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can the escalation go to a team rather than a named person? Because "assign to CSM" breaks the moment someone changes role.
[11:47] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): That happens constantly.
[11:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then route to a group, resolve dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And run history persists so you can see the inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.
[12:04] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): What happens when the workflow makes a bad call? Flags something that's fine.
[12:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a good question and the honest answer is you need a feedback path or the thing degrades. If a CSM dismisses a flag, that dismissal should be recorded, and you should look at dismissal rates as a health metric for the workflow itself.
[...]
[12:33] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You build it. It's a field on the task and a report. I'm not going to tell you there's a built-in model-monitoring feature, because there isn't.
[...]
[13:25] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's fine, I don't read it either.
[13:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Well, that's clarifying.
[13:32] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): The links back are the important part and I'm glad you specified them. The way we'd build it is that the source references are stored alongside the generated output, so whoever reads the summary can click through to the tickets that produced each claim.

COMPANY SIZE: 800 employees
STAGE: Churn post-mortem
DURATION: 21 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:

- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Kwame Boateng, Head of Operations, Verity Payments

TRANSCRIPT
[02:52] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Nobody in operations ever built anything.
[...]
[03:21] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [crosstalk] So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.
[...]
[03:45] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The first workflow anyone builds is hard. Not conceptually hard — fiddly. You have to understand connections, you have to understand how data moves between steps, you have to understand what happens when something's null. My operations people are good at operations. They're not good at that, and expecting them to become good at it in their spare time was naive.
[...]
[04:13] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We had a two-day onboarding at the start. Eight people attended. Six of them never touched it again.
[...]
[04:24] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Nothing, until you arrived in January and offered some sessions.
[...]
[04:31] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Which I declined, because by January I'd already half-concluded it wasn't going to work and I didn't want to spend my team's time on it.
[...]
[04:56] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Honestly, I think if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.
[...]

[05:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Then you've designed a product that fails by default for people like me.
[...]
[06:19] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations. [...]
[06:41] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] And because two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
[...]
[08:05] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] Yes. That's fair. We've bought an engineering tool and stopped pretending.
[...]
[09:06] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We never had that and I never asked for it, because I thought the product removed the need for it.
[...]
[09:34] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): We do say that, in fairness. It's in the operating model guidance.
[...]
[10:22] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): It's not that you lied. You just believed me, and you shouldn't have, because I didn't know what I was agreeing to.
[...]

[11:23] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): I assumed as much. It's not why we left. But it contributed to a general feeling that we were a small account.
[...]
[11:36] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] Probably accurately, yes.
[11:40] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's the answer, isn't it. You were an eighty-thousand-pound account in a book of accounts where that's below median.
[...]
[12:46] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] Ah.
[12:49] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): That's when it was over, if you want the specific moment.
[12:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Did anyone from our side know about the connector problem in April?
[12:59] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): I mentioned it on a call. Not as an emergency. As a thing I was dealing with.
[13:06] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I remember that call.
[13:08] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): You said you'd look into whether there was a template.
[13:12] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And I did, and there wasn't, and I emailed you saying there wasn't.
[13:18] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): You did. That was an accurate and completely useless answer.
[13:23] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] Yes. It was.
[13:26] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): I'm not attacking you. You answered the question I asked. It's just that the right response wasn't answering the question.
[13:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The right response was three days of an SE.
[13:40] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): The right response was three days of an SE, yes.
[13:44] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would we have done that?
[13:46] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): For an eighty-thousand-pound account at renewal risk? [pause] I'd have had to argue for it. I might have lost.
[13:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a thing I'm going to raise internally.
[13:59] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): For what it's worth, I don't think you should have kept us. I think we were the wrong customer for the product, or the product was sold to us for the wrong reason.
[...]
[16:09] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): There are two workflows still running that we haven't migrated. They'll be done by mid-October.
[...]
[16:18] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Merchant onboarding notifications and a daily reconciliation report.
[...]
[16:28] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The reconciliation one would be noticed. Not catastrophically.
[16:33] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'll flag them so nobody deactivates anything early.
[16:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask one more question and then I'll let you go?
[16:42] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Go on.
[16:44] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): If you were advising another operations director who was about to buy a workflow platform — any workflow platform, not ours — what would you tell them?
[16:56] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] Three things. First, name the person who'll build the fifth workflow, not the first. The first one gets built by whoever's enthusiastic. The fifth one gets built by whoever's job it is.
[17:12] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's better than my version of that question.
[17:16] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Second — do the integration assessment before you buy, not after. We spent four months discovering that our most important integration didn't exist. That's a question you can answer in a week if you insist on it during the evaluation.
[17:34] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): We should have insisted.
[17:37] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We should have insisted and we didn't, because everyone was excited.
[17:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And the third?
[17:44] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Third — be honest about whether you're buying a business tool or an engineering tool, because they're priced differently and they succeed differently, and if you buy one and use the other you'll be unhappy for two years.
[18:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the whole thing, isn't it.
[18:03] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): That's the whole thing.
[18:06] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Can I add one for the record?
[18:09] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[18:11] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Whatever platform you buy, get the exported definition of a real workflow during the evaluation and have an engineer read it. Not the demo. A real one, with branching. Because that tells you whether you'll be able to review changes, and it takes ten minutes, and almost nobody does it.
[18:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Someone did that to us last month, actually.
[18:37] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Did we pass?
[18:39] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] I think so. It's ongoing.
[18:43] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Good.
[18:45] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what would bring you back? In three years, at another company or here.
[18:52] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): An honest answer to "who will build the fifth workflow", and a proposal that includes whatever it costs to make that person real. If someone had said to me "this is eighty thousand for the platform and twenty-five for six months of someone sitting with your team", I might have said no. But I'd have said no with my eyes open, or said yes and it would have worked.
[...]
[19:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right. What you'll get from us — the run events API pagination details, read-only access through November, the deletion certificate with an actual timeline, and a note flagging the two live workflows so nothing gets switched off early.
[...]
[20:12] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd like to send you what I write up, if that's alright. So you can tell me if I've misrepresented anything.

=== CALL-015 (call kind: churn)
CALL ID: CALL-015
DATE: 2026-09-22
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Oakhill Property
INDUSTRY: Property management
COMPANY SIZE: 240 employees
STAGE: Churn post-mortem
DURATION: 13 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Alastair McCrae, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Hazel Wren, Operations Director, Oakhill Property
TRANSCRIPT
[01:23] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Four. And two of those only looked at reports.
[...]
[01:42] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): They worked perfectly. That's the frustrating part. I've got no complaint about the product at all.
[...]
[02:34] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a hard argument to counter.
[02:37] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): It's an impossible argument to counter. And I'd like to say — I did think about it properly. I'm not being flippant. I sat down and listed what we'd lose.
[02:50] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What was on the list?
[02:52] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): The run history. The approval forms, because our contractor sign-off uses those and Zapier can't really do it. And the fact that when something breaks, I know within an hour rather than when a tenant rings up.
[03:09] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Those are the three things that matter.
[03:12] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): They're the three things that matter and they're worth something. They're not worth nineteen thousand pounds a year to a company our size.
[03:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Alastair, do you want to come in?
[03:25] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yeah — Hazel, I mean, I'm sorry it's ended up here. Is there — I mean, is there a version where we look at the pricing? Because I could go and —
[03:37] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Alastair, no. I'm not doing that.
[03:41] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No, I understand, I just —
[03:44] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): If you can do it for eight thousand now, that tells me you could have done it for eight thousand two years ago, and then I'd be quite cross.
[03:54] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's fair.
[03:57] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Hazel, can I ask about the original purchase?
[04:01] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): You can, and Alastair may not enjoy it.
[04:05] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's fine. Honestly.
[04:08] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): When we bought this, I was told it would scale with us. That we'd start with the fault-reporting workflow and then do compliance, and then service charges, and then contractor management. And that was true — it would have. But we never did any of it.
[04:28] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Why not?
[04:30] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Because we're two hundred and forty people and everyone's already got a job. The roadmap I agreed to in the sales process assumed a version of Oakhill that spent time on process improvement, and we've never once had that time.
[04:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Was that discussed?
[04:49] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): It was discussed enthusiastically.
[04:52] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] By whom?
[04:55] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): By both of us, to be fair. I was enthusiastic too. I'm not putting this all on Alastair.
[05:03] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I did — I mean, I remember that conversation and you were quite keen on the compliance one.
[05:11] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I was extremely keen on the compliance one. I've been keen on the compliance one for three years. It has never once reached the top of my list.
[05:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So the purchase was priced against a future that didn't happen.
[05:27] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Yes. That's a good way of putting it. We paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty.
[05:37] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Is there anything we could have done?
[05:40] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] Yes, actually. Two things.
[05:44] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[05:46] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Someone should have noticed after six months that we had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something. Not sold me something. Said something.
[05:58] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a fair criticism. We look at that data.
[06:03] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Do you?
[06:04] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): We look at it. Whether anyone acts on it for an account your size is a different question, and the answer is usually no.
[06:14] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): At least you're honest.
[06:16] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What's the second thing?
[06:19] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): There should be a smaller plan. Something for a company that needs five workflows and three users and doesn't need thirty seats. If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer and I'd probably have done the compliance one eventually.
[06:39] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): There isn't one.
[06:41] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I know there isn't. Alastair told me at the time.
[06:45] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I did say that.
[06:47] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): You did say that, in fairness. You said the entry point is Growth and that's the entry point.
[06:54] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Did you consider not buying?
[06:57] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I did. And I decided the fault-reporting problem was bad enough to justify it, which it was. For about a year.
[07:07] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What changed after a year?
[07:10] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Nothing changed. That's the thing. It kept working. But the pain it solved stopped being fresh, and the invoice kept arriving, and eventually somebody looks at a renewal and asks what this is for.
[07:26] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): The problem being solved becomes invisible.
[07:30] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): The problem being solved becomes invisible. Exactly that. Nobody remembers how bad it was.
[07:38] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Do you think you'll regret it?
[07:41] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] Possibly. I think there'll be a moment in about four months when something breaks and nobody notices for two days and I'll think, well, that used to be handled.
[...]
[08:19] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Fine. Genuinely fine. I think I've raised two tickets in two years and both were answered.
[...]
[08:45] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] I'm going to be direct with you. Your account was in a segment that doesn't get an assigned CSM. I'm on this call because it's a churn, not because I've been managing you.
[08:59] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I'd worked that out. You've been very good today but you clearly hadn't heard of us before Tuesday.
[09:07] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Monday, actually.
[09:09] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [laughs] Monday.
[09:12] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'm not going to pretend otherwise.
[09:15] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I don't mind. It's a commercial reality. But it does rather answer the question of why nobody noticed the four users.
[09:25] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It does.
[09:27] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I say something?
[09:29] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Go on.
[09:31] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I think — looking back, I probably should have pushed harder on whether you had the capacity for the roadmap we talked about. I was excited about it and you were excited about it and neither of us asked who was actually going to do it.
[09:49] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] That's a good thing to say.
[09:53] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've been thinking about it since Ruth sent me the notice.
[09:58] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): For what it's worth, Alastair, I don't think you did anything wrong. You sold me a good product that does what it says. I just bought more of it than I needed.
[...]
[10:18] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Our workflow definitions, if only so I know how to rebuild them in Zapier.
[...]
[11:03] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] Possibly, actually. There's a Building Safety Act angle on fault response times.
[...]
[11:31] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Everyone does. And I'll arrange a deletion confirmation for afterwards with an actual date on it.

answer.summary: In both churn post-mortems, the departing customers said OrbitFlow could have helped earlier and more concretely: Verity wanted hands-on SE time in the first quarter and a more explicit commercial offer that included implementation help, while Oakhill wanted someone to notice low adoption sooner and to offer a smaller, cheaper plan that fit their actual usage. Both also said OrbitFlow should have pushed harder on capacity/readiness for the roadmap before the sale.

It's in the system.
[00:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): But?
[00:59] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): But supervisors still coordinate the remediation through phone calls and spreadsheets. So we can see the problem in three different dashboards and the actual fixing of it happens over the phone.

[01:17] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): It's absolutely not a visibility problem. We've got more visibility than we know what to do with. It's a — I don't know what you'd call it.
[01:27] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): It's a coordination problem.
[01:29] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): It's a coordination problem, yeah. Nothing moves the work along.
[01:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's actually a distinction I wish more people made. We see two separate things — connecting systems, which you've largely done, and operating the process on top of the connections, which is where the pain usually sits.
[01:50] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Then you've got us.
[01:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How long does a blocked installation typically sit?
[01:57] Carlos Mendes (Head of Digital Operations, Greenline Energy Services): Depends who's on. Some supervisors are brilliant and it's an hour. Others, it's two days.
[02:05] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): That variance is the actual problem, I'd say. It's not that the average is bad. It's that we can't predict it.
[02:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you have numbers?
[02:16] Lucy Hart (Field Systems Product Manager, Greenline Energy Services): Some. We have outcome metrics — installations completed, first-time-fix rate, that sort of thing. The answer weighs both sides and concludes SSO is Enterprise-only, not on Growth.

[01:02] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right. Sharing. [pause] Can you see it?
[01:07] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Yep.
[01:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So this is the workflow builder. Triggers and actions on the left, the flow in the middle, and whatever step you've clicked gets its config on the right.
[01:20] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've pre-built something that I think is roughly your world. High-value order comes in, there's a fulfilment exception on it, we open a ticket, we ping a channel, we update a tracker.
[01:34] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): That's — yeah, that's almost exactly it. Detect high-value orders with fulfilment exceptions, Zendesk ticket, right Slack channel, and update our Airtable exception tracker.
[01:48] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let me just run it. [pause] So it's triggered off the order event, it checks the value threshold, it checks the exception flag, and then it branches.
[02:01] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Stop there. What happens if the order data's incomplete?

[02:17] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Owned by who?

[02:53] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): When a customer complains.
[02:56] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] Right.
[02:59] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): That's not a joke, that's genuinely the detection mechanism.
[03:04] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): It's the honest answer.
[03:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's a very common answer. It's just usually not said out loud in the first ten minutes.
[03:14] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Well, we're not going to fix it by pretending.

[03:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes — you can alert when error rates cross a threshold. And that's the right instinct, everyone who alerts per-failure ends up ignoring all of them.
[04:01] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Learned that one the hard way.
[04:05] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Can I correct something Sophie said in the email, actually?
[04:09] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Go on.

Support feels like the loudest problem because failures surface there — that's where the customer shouts. But honestly, probably only about a quarter of the automations actually touch Zendesk.
[04:31] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a really useful correction. What do the other three quarters touch?
[04:37] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Shopify mostly. Klaviyo. Some Airtable stuff.
[04:42] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Let me give you the full list. Shopify, Zendesk, Klaviyo, Slack, Airtable, and Zapier holding it all together with string.
[04:53] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And of those, which one is the one that has to work perfectly?
[04:58] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Shopify. A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
